content: The document is a systematic review and meta-analysis conducted by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2021. It evaluates the performance of vaginal discharge syndromic management in diagnosing and treating vaginal and cervical infections. 1. Purpose of the Review: The review aimed to assess the diagnostic accuracy of syndromic management algorithms for vaginal discharge in identifying vaginal and cervical infections. These infections include those caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae (NG), Chlamydia trachomatis (CT), Trichomonas vaginalis (TV), and bacterial vaginosis (BV). 2. Search Strategy and Study Selection: The systematic review updated a previous analysis by Zemouri (2016). The search was extended to include studies published between January 2015 and September 2018. Databases such as OVID Medline, CENTRAL, and EMBASE were used. Studies were included if they evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of vaginal discharge flowcharts compared to laboratory diagnostic tests. Only studies in English, French, Spanish, or Dutch were considered. Case reports and letters to the editor were excluded. 3. Inclusion Criteria: Studies were included if they provided data on sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive values (PPV), and negative predictive values (NPV) or if these parameters could be calculated from two-by-two tables. Studies that did not differentiate between cervical and vaginal infections were excluded. 4. Flowchart Categorization: The review categorized flowcharts into four types: Flowchart 1: Based on history and risk assessment. Flowchart 2: Includes history, risk assessment, and speculum examination. Flowchart 3: Adds vaginal discharge sampling for Gram staining and microscopy. Flowchart 4: Country-adapted flowcharts or other combinations of screening methods. 5. Statistical Analysis: A meta-analysis was conducted by pooling data from studies using different types of flowcharts. If a study presented separate results for NG, CT, TV, and BV, the one with the highest PPV was included to avoid overrepresentation. 6. Risk of Bias Assessment: The QUADAS-2 tool was used to evaluate the risk of bias in included studies. Bias was assessed in four domains: patient selection, index test, reference standard, and flow/timing. Studies were graded as having high, low, or unclear risk of bias. 7. Results: A total of 1,569 citations were identified, with 1,258 remaining after removing duplicates. After screening, 173 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility, and four new studies were included in the updated review. These four studies added 2,240 participants to the analysis, bringing the total to 20 studies with 12,778 participants. 8. Study Characteristics: The newly included studies validated different types of flowcharts for diagnosing vaginal and cervical infections. For example: Barry (2018) validated a single flowchart for both cervical and vaginal infections. Bannaheke (2016) focused on vaginal infections caused by TV. Molaei (2018) assessed diagnostic methods for BV. Vallely (2017) evaluated flowcharts for both cervical and vaginal infections, specifically for TV. 9. Diagnostic Validity: The pooled diagnostic validity of the flowcharts was analyzed separately for cervical infections (NG and CT) and vaginal infections (BV and TV). The performance of each flowchart type was compared to laboratory-based diagnostic standards. 10. General Findings: Syndromic management algorithms showed variable diagnostic accuracy depending on the type of infection and the flowchart used. The inclusion of speculum examination and laboratory tests (e.g., Gram staining) improved diagnostic accuracy. Country-adapted flowcharts demonstrated potential for improving diagnostic outcomes in specific settings. 11. Limitations: The review excluded studies published in languages other than English, French, Spanish, and Dutch. There was a high risk of bias in some studies, particularly in patient selection and reference standards. 12. Conclusion: The updated systematic review highlights the strengths and limitations of syndromic management for vaginal discharge. While it remains a practical approach in resource-limited settings, its diagnostic accuracy varies, and laboratory confirmation is often necessary for optimal management. This document is part of the WHO guidelines for managing symptomatic sexually transmitted infections and is intended to provide transparency and evidence-based recommendations for clinical practice.
